title: Humanitarian principles
description: A workshop on humanity, neutrality, impartiality, independence, and responsible civic action.
discussionQuestions: How do principles help protect access?
What does impartiality require in public communication?
actionExercise: Rewrite an advocacy statement so every claim is sourced and civilian-centered.
copyableText: Humanitarian action should prioritize human need, dignity, impartiality, and accountable support channels.

title: International humanitarian law and civilian protection
description: Introduces civilian protection, medical protection, humanitarian access, and limits on tactics.
discussionQuestions: Why does civilian protection apply across identities?
What should a civic briefing avoid claiming without legal review?
actionExercise: Create a one-page source-based brief on civilian protection concerns.
copyableText: Civilian protection language must be careful, sourced, and reviewed before public use.

title: Aid accountability and transparency
description: Explains how evidence supports responsible giving without ratings or certification.
discussionQuestions: What evidence is enough for routing support?
Why are rankings avoided?
actionExercise: Compare two transparency passports and identify missing evidence.
copyableText: Evidence language helps users see what is confirmed, partial, missing, under review, or not applicable.

title: Conflict transformation
description: Connects humanitarian response to relationships, systems, history, and long-term repair.
discussionQuestions: What changes if food assistance is viewed through dignity?
What future pattern should action interrupt?
actionExercise: Map one sector across immediate need, relationship repair, and institutional trust.
copyableText: Conflict transformation asks how action reduces harm now while changing conditions that reproduce harm.

title: Mediation and negotiation
description: Introduces interests, positions, guarantees, implementation, and verification.
discussionQuestions: What makes access agreements fragile?
How can outside advocacy avoid oversimplification?
actionExercise: Identify stakeholders, interests, constraints, and possible confidence-building measures.
copyableText: Negotiation analysis helps explain why access, protection, and recovery depend on sustained arrangements.

title: Complexity and polarization
description: Shows how systems feedback and polarized narratives can trap communities in recurring harm.
discussionQuestions: Which feedback loop links WASH and health?
How can language reduce polarization?
actionExercise: Draw a simple systems loop for one sector and identify a leverage point.
copyableText: Complex crises require humility, source discipline, and attention to unintended consequences.

title: Trauma-informed peacebuilding
description: Explores safety, grief, agency, memory, and psychosocial repair.
discussionQuestions: How can help become extractive?
What does grief-sensitive education require?
actionExercise: Design a workshop rule set that protects dignity and prevents performative storytelling.
copyableText: Trauma-informed action supports safety, choice, collaboration, trust, and empowerment.

title: Intergroup contact and reconciliation
description: Examines conditions for contact, acknowledgment, justice, and coexistence.
discussionQuestions: When is dialogue inappropriate?
What must be true for contact to reduce harm?
actionExercise: Draft safeguards for a campus dialogue event.
copyableText: Dialogue requires credible facilitation, safety, and a clear distinction from propaganda.

title: Responsible action without manipulation
description: Helps students and institutions act without unsupported claims, exploitation, or direct-risk pathways.
discussionQuestions: What makes an action pathway manipulative?
How can urgency coexist with restraint?
actionExercise: Turn a viral claim into a verified, caveated briefing note.
copyableText: Responsible action routes support through accountable organizations and clearly names uncertainty.

title: How peacebuilding works across top, middle, and grassroots levels
description: Uses the Lederach pyramid to locate diplomacy, institutions, professional networks, and community work.
discussionQuestions: Which level can a university realistically support?
What bridge is missing between sectors?
actionExercise: Place each action card on the pyramid and identify dependencies.
copyableText: Peacebuilding works across levels; responsible support knows which level it is strengthening.

title: How students, universities, labs, and civic groups can help
description: Defines safe roles for learning, public data tools, workshops, and capacity support.
discussionQuestions: What should student projects never do?
How can a lab support without becoming operational?
actionExercise: Write a project charter with review gates, data limits, and partner accountability.
copyableText: Universities and labs can help through public-interest tools, workshops, and partner-requested capacity building.
